title: Perkins: assurance of remission is faith’s perfection, not its essence — weak implicit faith
source_text: XXXIII. Neque vero solus ille est qui putat certitudinem illam, quam quis habet de impetrata aut certo obtinenda remissione peccatorum suorum, non pertinere ad fidei salvificae essentiam, sed solum ad illius complementum & perfectionem. Id docet pluribus in locis Perkinsius, praesertim vero in controversia de fide implicita, quaestione sexta in Catholico ejus Reformato. Ubi dicit quendam esse fidei implicitae & indistinctae modum, respectu apprehensionis; quando nimirum, homo aliquis, nequit certo & distincte de se dicere, Credo ego remissionem peccatorum meorum: quod ait multis Dei filiis accidere, qui infima fide praediti sunt. Et tales habere fidem, sed implicitam, perinde atque in minuto aliquo & arido grano implicita sunt folia, flores & fructus; & Deum nihilominus hujusmodi fidem acceptare ad aeternam eorum salutem. Unde dicit declarandam esse Catechismorum quorundam institutionem, qui solent fidem in summo & perfectissimo sui gradu definire, dum eam esse dicunt certam atque completam mentis persuasionem de amore Dei & favore erga nos in Christo. Nam licet, inquit, omnis fides ex natura sua certa sit persuasio, sola tamen perfecta persuasio est firma & consummata fides. Ac proinde debebat fides definiri, non solum in genere & secundum summum, sed etiam variis ejus gradibus & mensuris declarari, ut & qui infirmi sunt, vere & recte de suo statu possint edoceri. Quod idem author prolixe confirmat in tractatu cui titulum fecit Granum sinapis; ubi postquam asserit firmam fidem illam esse, quae plenam apprehensionem, & Dei in Christo misericordiae persuasionem efficit & operatur: & omnibus hoc non esse concessum; ideoque esse gradum fidei inferiorem, qui vera fides est, licet infirma atque exigua, subjungit verba sequentia, Quicunque autem hanc infirmam fidem habent, possunt vere affirmare se credere omnia sua peccata esse remissibilia: Et quod eorum condemnationem oderunt, sed huc usque ea esse remissa sine dubitatione affirmare non audent; nihilominus divina misericordia eos non deficit aut destituit. In cujus rei confirmationem profert testimonia Bradfordi, Knoxii, Tassini & aliorum. In explicatione & probatione tertiae Theseos.
pass_a_gloss: Nor indeed is he alone who thinks that that certainty which someone has concerning remission of his sins obtained or certainly to be obtained does not pertain to the essence of saving faith, but only to its complement and perfection. Perkins teaches this in several places, but especially in the controversy on implicit faith, the sixth question in his Reformed Catholic. Where he says there is a certain mode of implicit and indistinct faith with respect to apprehension; when namely someone cannot surely and distinctly say of himself, I believe the remission of my sins: which he says happens to many sons of God who are endowed with the lowest faith. And that such have faith, but implicit, just as in some tiny and dry grain leaves, flowers and fruits are implicit; and that God nevertheless accepts such faith unto their eternal salvation. Whence he says the teaching of certain Catechisms is to be clarified, which are wont to define faith in its highest and most perfect degree, when they say it is a sure and complete persuasion of the mind concerning God's love and favor toward us in Christ. For although, he says, every faith is by its nature a sure persuasion, yet only perfect persuasion is firm and consummate faith. And therefore faith ought to be defined not only in general and according to the highest, but also to be declared in its various degrees and measures, so that those who are weak also may be truly and rightly taught about their state. Which the same author confirms at length in the treatise to which he gave the title Grain of Mustard Seed; where after he asserts that firm faith is that which effects and works full apprehension and persuasion of God's mercy in Christ: and that this is not granted to all; and therefore there is a lower degree of faith which is true faith, though weak and small, he subjoins the following words: But whoever have this weak faith can truly affirm that they believe all their sins are remissible: And that they hate their condemnation, but thus far they dare not affirm without doubt that they have been remitted; nevertheless the divine mercy does not fail or forsake them. In confirmation of which he brings the testimonies of Bradford, Knox, Tassin and others. In the explanation and proof of the third Thesis.
pass_b_english: Wittich is not alone: certainty of obtained/coming remission is complement of saving faith, not essence.
Perkins (Reformed Catholic, implicit faith q.6): weak sons of God may not distinctly say ‘I believe my sins remitted’.
Yet they have true implicit faith — like leaves/flowers latent in a dry grain; God accepts it unto salvation.
Catechisms that define faith only as complete persuasion of God’s love miss lower true degrees.
Mustard-seed: weak faith believes sins remissible and hates condemnation — without yet daring full ‘remitted’ certainty.

lemmas.gloss: does not pertain to the essence of saving faith, but only to its complement and perfection

choices.english: yet only perfect persuasion is firm and consummate faith

rejected: Perkins makes complete assurance essential to any saving faith
